message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) belong to two very different orders—Carnivora for lions and Perissodactyla for zebras.  
Their most recent common ancestor is therefore a member of the larger clade **Laurasiatheria**, the group that gave rise to many modern land mammals such as ungulates, carnivores, bats, and whales.

**Key points**

| Group | Order | Last common ancestor with the other |
|-------|-------|-------------------------------------|
| Lion | Carnivora | ~55–60 million years ago (Paleocene/Eocene) |
| Zebra | Perissodactyla | ~55–60 million years ago (Paleocene/Eocene) |

So the last common ancestor of lions and zebras was a small, insectivorous‑to‑omnivorous mammal that lived roughly 55–60 million years ago, sometime after the split of the Laurasiatherian lineages that led to the modern orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla. It would have resembled a tiny, shrew‑like creature, though its exact morphology is unknown because no fossils have been found that definitively link the two lineages.
